title: Barley water recorded in 1920
recorded_method: The barley was washed and soaked for several hours in the measured cold water.
It was then boiled gently in the same water for 2 hours.
The source also offered a double-boiler method: 4 hours of cooking, or until the liquid was reduced by half.
source_fit: Direct period match for the archived preparation. This American cookbook printed the measured formula under “Invalid Cookery”; that placement documents historical use, not medical effectiveness.
archive_note: Optional lemon juice, sugar, or salt were mentioned only “to taste” in the source, so they are not listed as measured ingredients here.
safety_notes: Barley contains gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease.
This is a food-history record, not a substitute for medical care or an oral rehydration solution.
It should not be used as infant formula or as a substitute for breast milk or commercial infant formula.
If retained after cooking, it should be refrigerated within 2 hours and discarded after 3 to 4 days.

title: Cup of arrowroot recorded in 1897
recorded_method: A little of the measured cold milk was used to work the arrowroot into a smooth paste.
The remaining milk was boiled and poured onto the paste while it was stirred smooth.
If it had not thickened enough, it was returned to the saucepan and stirred over the heat for another 2 to 3 minutes.
source_fit: Exact period preparation match, but not a direct source for the archived entry’s American cultural attribution. The source is a British Jewish cookbook and is cited only for the measured method.
archive_note: The historical unit “dessertspoonful” is preserved exactly because period spoon measures were not fully standardized; no modern conversion has been guessed. Sugar or salt were optional and unmeasured in the source.
safety_notes: Only pasteurized milk should be used; raw milk can carry harmful germs.
This preparation contains milk and is not suitable for anyone with a milk allergy.
It should not be used as infant formula or as a substitute for breast milk or commercial infant formula; cow's milk should not be introduced as a drink before 12 months.
If retained after cooking, it should be refrigerated within 2 hours and discarded after 3 to 4 days.

title: Rice-water recorded in 1893
recorded_method: The rice was picked over and washed.
It was put into a saucepan with the measured boiling water and simmered for 2 hours, until the rice was softened and partly dissolved.
The liquid was strained through a fine wire strainer into a bowl or pitcher.
The measured salt was added, and the rice-water was served warm or cold.
source_fit: Exact period match for a measured rice-water preparation in an American nursing handbook. It does not independently verify the archived entry’s Gullah or Lowcountry attribution, nor does it establish treatment effectiveness.
archive_note: The source suggested fortified wine as an optional addition in some circumstances. That optional alcohol was omitted from this archive formula and is not needed to reproduce the base rice-water recipe.
safety_notes: Rice-water is not an oral rehydration solution: it does not contain the verified glucose-and-electrolyte balance used to replace losses from diarrhea.
Children with diarrhea should be discussed with a health professional; infants should continue breast milk or formula as advised by their clinician.
This historical food preparation is not infant formula and is not a treatment for dehydration or diarrhea.
If retained after cooking, it should be refrigerated within 2 hours and discarded after 3 to 4 days.

title: Beef broth recorded in 1893
recorded_method: The meat was cleaned and divided into half-inch pieces to expose more surface to the water.
It was placed in a granite-ware kettle with the measured cold water and cooked at a low temperature for 2 hours.
The broth was then boiled for 2 hours.
It was strained through a coarse wire strainer and the fat was skimmed from the surface.
source_fit: Direct period match for the archived entry’s cooked beef-broth method. The source documents an American nursing-food formula; it does not validate modern “bone broth” claims or prove medical effectiveness.
archive_note: Salt and pepper were specified only as seasoning, without measurements, so they are not listed as measured ingredients. The source’s separate raw and acidified beef-tea methods were excluded.
safety_notes: Raw beef should be kept separate from ready-to-eat foods, and hands, utensils, and surfaces should be cleaned after handling it.
A food thermometer should be used to verify that meat reaches a safe minimum internal temperature; the historical cooking time alone is not a modern safety check.
If retained after cooking, broth should be refrigerated within 2 hours and discarded after 3 to 4 days.
This is a food-history record, not a medical treatment or a nutritionally complete diet.

title: Chicken broth recorded in 1884
recorded_method: Half of the chicken was chopped into pieces and placed in a small saucepan.
The measured cold water and celery leaf were added, and the mixture was simmered gently for 2 hours.
Oily particles were removed thoroughly and the broth was strained into a bowl.
The source recorded serving the broth after it had cooled slightly, with the cooked meat alongside it.
source_fit: A measured American period formula for chicken broth served to a convalescent. It does not independently verify the archived entry’s Ashkenazi attribution, Maimonides narrative, vegetable list, or medical effectiveness.
archive_note: The source called for “a little salt” without a measurement, so salt is not listed as a measured ingredient. The period description “dry-picked Philadelphia roasting chicken” is preserved in the citation context but not treated as a required modern product.
safety_notes: Chicken should reach a safe minimum internal temperature of 165°F, verified with a food thermometer.
Raw poultry should be kept separate from ready-to-eat foods, and hands, utensils, and surfaces should be cleaned after handling it.
If retained after cooking, broth should be refrigerated within 2 hours and discarded after 3 to 4 days.
Chicken broth may be food, but this historical formula is not medical treatment and should not replace needed clinical care.

title: Flaxseed tea with lemon recorded in 1893
recorded_method: The flaxseed was examined and any stray dark grains were removed.
The measured flaxseed was boiled in the measured water for 1 hour.
The liquid was strained, then the measured lemon juice and sugar were added.
The source recorded serving the preparation either warm or cold.
source_fit: A complete measured American period formula for a flaxseed mucilage drink. It supports the general preparation method but does not independently verify the archived entry’s Polish attribution, its honey variation, or treatment effectiveness.
archive_note: The period source called this “Flaxseed Tea with Lemon.” Its respiratory claims are preserved only as historical context and are not presented as evidence that the drink treats croup or lung disease.
safety_notes: Only ripe, food-grade flaxseed should be used; raw or unripe flaxseed may contain potentially toxic compounds.
Flaxseed can cause bloating, fullness, or diarrhea, and it may interact with medicines, including anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs.
Flaxseed should be avoided during pregnancy, and safety while breastfeeding is not established.
This historical drink is not a treatment for croup or breathing difficulty; urgent breathing symptoms need prompt medical care.

title: Lemon whey recorded in 1880

ingredients.item: pasteurized milk, brought to a boil (modern substitute for the source’s “new milk”)

recorded_method: The measured lemon juice was stirred into the measured boiling-hot milk.
The mixture was simmered very gently until the whey separated from the curd.
The clear whey was strained from the curd and sweetened with the measured sugar.
The source recorded a total preparation time of about 10 minutes.
source_fit: Direct American period match for the archived entry’s strained, acid-curdled whey drink. It verifies the measured preparation, not the entry’s fever claim, Shakespeare reference, or medical effectiveness.
archive_note: The source called for “new milk,” which in 1880 could mean fresh unpasteurized milk. The measured formula is preserved, but pasteurized milk is specified here as a modern food-safety substitution. The same source printed wine and vinegar variants; the nonalcoholic lemon formula was selected.
safety_notes: Only pasteurized milk should be used; raw milk can carry harmful germs.
This preparation contains milk and is not suitable for anyone with a milk allergy.
It should not be used as infant formula or as a substitute for breast milk or commercial infant formula.
If retained after preparation, it should be refrigerated within 2 hours and discarded after 3 to 4 days.

title: Irish moss blanc-mange recorded in 1880

ingredients.item: pasteurized milk, brought to a boil (modern substitute for the source’s “new milk”)

recorded_method: The Irish moss was washed, soaked in a little cold water for 5 minutes, and removed from the soaking water.
It was added to the measured boiling-hot milk and simmered until the liquid had approximately the consistency of cream.
The measured sugar and vanilla were added, and the mixture was strained through a wire sieve into a mould to cool.
Once cold, the blanc-mange was turned out onto a dish; the source recorded a total preparation time of about 45 minutes.
source_fit: Direct American period match for the archived entry’s Irish-moss-and-milk preparation. It verifies a measured historical food formula, not the entry’s cough or convalescence claims or medical effectiveness.
archive_note: The source called for “new milk,” so pasteurized milk is specified as a modern food-safety substitution. It also suggested additional cream and sugar for serving without quantities; those optional additions are not included in the measured list.
safety_notes: Use only commercially sold food-grade Irish moss, not unidentified or roadside-harvested seaweed.

Seaweed can contain substantial and variable iodine. People with thyroid disease, those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and people taking thyroid or iodine-related medicines should ask a qualified clinician before consuming concentrated seaweed preparations.
Only pasteurized milk should be used, and the preparation is not suitable for anyone with a milk allergy.
This is a historical food record, not a treatment for cough, lung disease, or recovery from illness.
